title: The garland on the hunter's head
hookLine: Arjuna fights the hunter with everything he has and loses, then lays a garland before Shiva and sees it on the hunter's head
carry: what's offered with love reaches god

cards: Everything Arjuna has, he throws at the hunter. This is the great archer, carrying the bow Gandiva and quivers the epic describes as never running out. He looses a storm of arrows.
The hunter simply stands there and takes them, unhurt, the way a mountain takes rain. Arjuna shoots and shoots, and then something happens he didn't expect. He reaches back, and the quiver is empty.

teach.h: THE BOW TAKEN, THE SWORD BROKEN.
teach.b: So Arjuna fights with whatever is left. He strikes with the end of his bow, and the hunter snatches it away. He brings his sword down on the hunter's head, and the sword breaks.
They wrestle, and the hunter presses him so hard that Arjuna falls senseless to the ground. Everything his austerities built, the strength, the focus, the pride, has failed.
Then, coming to, Arjuna does what he came to the mountain for. He stops fighting and turns to worship.
He shapes an altar from earth, honors Shiva upon it, and lays a garland of flowers there. When he looks up, he sees the garland. It's on the hunter's head.

Arjuna understands who has been standing in front of him all along, falls at Shiva's feet and asks forgiveness, and Shiva, pleased, praises his courage. Now the teaching. Tapas made Arjuna strong; it didn't make him see.
What opened his eyes was one humble offering, and it went straight to the god.

teach.h: A LEAF, A FLOWER, A LITTLE WATER.
teach.b: In the Bhagavad Gita, Krishna says it plainly: offer me a leaf, a flower, a fruit, a little water, with devotion, and I accept it.

teach.h: THE GARLAND ON THE HUNTER'S HEAD.
teach.b: That's bhakti, devotion, and it's why a Hindu home begins the day with a flower at the shrine. Not because God needs flowers; because the offering turns the one who offers.
For today: the thing you've been fighting alone can be offered too.

how: Devotees of Shiva retell Arjuna's defeat and recognition as the god meeting his worshipper in disguise, and Hindu homes still begin worship by offering a flower, which the Gita says is accepted when given with devotion.

o: the garland laid on an altar made of earth
a wrestling contest between Arjuna and a god
Arjuna's hard discipline, ending in a lost fight

games.q: the fight on the mountain — tap the pairs.

s: Arjuna defeated the hunter and then learned he was Shiva
Arjuna lost: his bow was taken, his sword broke, and he fell senseless.
Arjuna recognized Shiva by a garland he had offered
he laid it on an earthen altar to Shiva and then saw it on the hunter's head.
in Hindu worship, an offering only counts if it's big and costly
in the Gita, Krishna accepts a leaf, a flower, a fruit or a little water, offered with devotion.

games.q: you've been fighting something hard for weeks, and it won't budge. by Arjuna's story, what does a Hindu reach for?
o: push harder, alone, until something breaks.
offer it: bring the struggle to the shrine with a flower or a prayer, and keep doing your part.
games.why: Arjuna's strength failed, but the garland he offered reached Shiva's own head. offering isn't quitting: he walked away with Shiva's blessing.

practice: If you have a home shrine, or just a windowsill, set down one small thing: a flower, a leaf, a little water in a cup. Bring to mind something you've been fighting hard alone.
Breathe in and feel how tired the fight has made you; breathe out and lay it down with your offering, the way Arjuna laid down his garland.
If you pray, say Shiva's name, or Om Namah Shivaya as many Hindus do, or the name you use for God; if not, simply set it down and rest.

wordCard.voice: Arjuna's austerities. They end in a lost fight, an altar of earth, and a garland found on the head of the hunter who was Shiva.

carryVoice: Your line: what's offered with love reaches God. The garland found its way to the right head. Day seven hundred eighty-five, done.

sources.ref: Mahabharata, Vana Parva (Aranyaka Parva), Kairata Parva (the fight with the Kirata; the empty quivers; Gandiva taken; Arjuna overpowered; worship with a garland; recognition of Shiva)
Bhagavad Gita 9.26 (a leaf, a flower, a fruit or water offered with devotion is accepted); offering flowers in daily home worship (puja)
